markingScheme.criterion: States the real property that makes the difference: the soil/mud in muddy water is an insoluble solid (undissolved particles too large to pass through filter paper), while salt in salt water has actually dissolved into individual particles too small for any filter paper to trap.
markingScheme.accept: Any correct statement that the muddy sample's solid has NOT dissolved (still separate particles) while the salt HAS dissolved, in the student's own words.
markingScheme.insufficient: Saying 'one is a mixture and one is a solution' with no explanation of why particle size/dissolving is the reason filtration works or fails.

markingScheme.criterion: Explains specifically why filter paper cannot catch a dissolved solute: filtration only traps solid particles that are physically too large to pass through the paper's tiny holes, and a dissolved solute's particles are far smaller than that, so they pass straight through with the water.
markingScheme.accept: Any correct statement that dissolved particles are small enough to pass through filter paper along with the solvent.
markingScheme.insufficient: Restating 'salt can't be filtered' without explaining why filter paper fails to trap it.

markingScheme.criterion: Gives a genuine real-life link: this is exactly why real water treatment plants use filtration to remove suspended mud/silt/debris from river water, but must use a different process (such as evaporation/distillation or chemical treatment) to remove dissolved substances like salts.
markingScheme.accept: Any real-world example of a water treatment or purification process that filters out suspended solids but needs a different method for dissolved substances.
markingScheme.insufficient: A generic statement like 'this is useful for cleaning water' with no real-world process named.

markingScheme.criterion: Correctly identifies magnetism as the method, because steel is magnetic and plastic is not — a magnet can pull the steel caps out of the mixed load while leaving the plastic flakes behind.
markingScheme.accept: Naming magnetism as the method with steel's magnetic property (or plastic's non-magnetic property) stated as the reason.

markingScheme.criterion: Explains why filtration would not work here (both plastic flakes and steel caps are solids of a similar kind, mixed dry together, not a solid-in-liquid mixture, so there is nothing for a filter paper to separate) and why evaporation would not work (neither substance is a solute dissolved in a solvent — there is no liquid to evaporate away).
markingScheme.accept: Either explanation alone still earns the mark if reasoned correctly from the real property involved; both together is not required, but the reasoning must be feature-based, not just 'those methods are for something else'.
markingScheme.insufficient: Saying 'filtration and evaporation wouldn't work' with no property-based reason given.

markingScheme.criterion: Gives a genuine real-life link: this is the same reasoning behind real recycling plants, which use large magnetic separators (magnetic drums or overhead magnets on conveyor belts) to automatically pull ferrous metal out of mixed waste streams before further sorting.
markingScheme.accept: Any real-world example of magnetic separation used in recycling, scrap sorting, or waste processing.
markingScheme.insufficient: A generic statement like 'this is useful for recycling' with no real-world magnetic-separation scenario named.

levels.descriptor: Achieves none of the three: does not identify dissolving/particle size as the deciding property, gives no explanation of why filter paper fails on a dissolved solute, and no real-life link is given.

Achieves only ONE of the three: identifies that the salt has dissolved while the mud has not OR explains why filter paper can't trap dissolved particles OR gives a genuine real-life water-treatment link — the other two are missing or incorrect.

Achieves TWO of the three: e.g. correctly identifies the dissolving/particle-size difference and explains why filter paper fails on a dissolved solute, but gives no real-life link (or identifies the difference and gives a real-life link, but does not explain why filter paper itself fails).

States that the mud is an undissolved insoluble solid while the salt has genuinely dissolved, explains that filter paper only traps particles too large to pass through its holes so a dissolved solute passes straight through, and gives a genuine real-life link to real water treatment processes — all three analytic points present.

levels.descriptor: Achieves none of the three: does not correctly identify magnetism as the method, gives no reasoning for why filtration/evaporation fail, and no real-life link is given.

Achieves only ONE of the three: correctly identifies magnetism using the magnetic/non-magnetic property OR explains why filtration and evaporation would not work OR gives a genuine real-life link to real recycling/scrap-sorting — the other two are missing or incorrect.

Achieves TWO of the three: e.g. correctly identifies magnetism and explains why the other two methods fail, but gives no real-life link (or identifies it and gives a real-life link, but the elimination reasoning for filtration/evaporation is missing).

Correctly identifies magnetism using steel's magnetic property, explains why filtration and evaporation would not work on this dry solid-solid mixture, and gives a genuine real-life link to real magnetic separation in recycling plants — all three analytic points present.

markingInstructions: Mark ONLY the two constructed responses (Explain, Apply). Award marks point-by-point using each question's markingScheme above: each point is worth the marks stated, is independent unless it names a dependsOn point (in which case only award it if that earlier point was also awarded), and each point's 'accept'/'insufficient' tell you exactly what does and doesn't count. use_of_evidence's 3 marks ARE the Explain markingScheme's 3 points, and reasoning's 3 marks ARE the Apply markingScheme's 3 points — the rubric levels restate the same points as bands; award each set of 3 marks ONCE, not twice. communication is a separate, holistic 2 marks across both answers' clarity and vocabulary, never overlapping with the content marks. Only cost a communication mark for spelling/grammar when it actually harms clarity, never for a minor slip alone. Copy auto_marked_score into knowledge_accuracy. Use the student's own logged results (the stage/sample/result columns in simulation_results.trials) to verify any sample or property they claim to reference — do not take their prose summary on trust if it does not match their own logged data. Accept valid alternative wording (e.g. 'won't dissolve' for 'insoluble', 'heating it dry' for 'evaporation'). Total is out of 15 (7 auto + 3 + 3 + 2). Report total, percentage, one strength, one correction, one next step, under 80 words.
